title: VHS to digital
meta_title: VHS to digital: what to know before you convert
meta_description: What VHS and VHS-C are, why damaged tapes should not go into a VCR, and what to ask a transfer shop before you pay.
lede: VHS is the large black cassette from the late 1970s through the 2000s. A useful transfer gives you a file you can copy, and it gives you the original tape back. A higher price does not recover picture detail the tape never recorded.

sections.heading: VHS and VHS-C
paragraphs: A common blank was labeled T-120, about two hours at the fastest speed families actually used. Many home recordings are longer because the camcorder or VCR was set to a slower speed. Ask the shop whether a long tape is one price or a price per hour.

VHS-C is the smaller cassette that fit in a camcorder. It is the same kind of tape. It plays in a full-size VHS deck with an adapter. Compact tapes are easier to jam. Tell the shop you have VHS-C so they do not quote you for a format they do not run.
S-VHS looks like VHS and is sharper. A deck that is only a consumer VHS machine may play it as ordinary VHS or not play it well. If the label says S-VHS, say so when you call.

sections.heading: What the picture can and cannot be
paragraphs: VHS is standard definition, on the order of 240 lines of detail, which is softer than a DVD. A careful transfer keeps the frames stable, keeps the audio in sync, and saves a file a modern TV or phone can open. Upscaling can make that file look a bit smoother on a large television. It does not invent faces, text, or color that the tape never held.

The file you want is a normal video file, usually MP4, that you can copy to a drive and to a second place outside your house. A DVD is fine as an extra for a living-room player. One DVD holds roughly two hours, and a recorded DVD is a weak only copy.

sections.heading: Do not play a sick tape
paragraphs: Binder breakdown, mold, and stretched tape are common in boxes that lived in a Texas attic or a damp garage. Warning signs are white or green fuzz on the tape pack, powder in the window, a musty smell, a door that will not open, or a squeal as soon as the tape moves.

Stop if you hear that squeal. A dirty or misaligned video head can scrape the magnetic coating off. Put the tape back in its case, keep it out of the attic, and take it to a shop that will inspect it before playback. Upright storage in a cool, dry room is the right holding pattern. This guide is not a repair manual.

sections.heading: What to ask, and what to pay attention to
bullets: Is the price per cassette or per minute, and what happens past two hours?
Do they inspect and, if needed, repair a snapped or moldy tape, and is that a separate fee?
Do you get an MP4 (or another file you can copy) and the original cassette?
How long is the current turnaround for the number of tapes you have?
Will they refuse copyrighted movies and recorded TV? They should.
paragraphs: Local Dallas–Fort Worth rates that shops actually publish are on the [Dallas–Fort Worth page](/vhsnearme/cities/dallas-fort-worth/). National kit and per-tape prices are on the [mail-in comparison](/vhsnearme/mail-in/). Those pages name the source for each number.
